reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: An IgE-mediated hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa presenting with sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, nasal itching and congestion
Often classified as seasonal (pollen-driven) or perennial (dust mite, animal dander, mould), and by severity and effect on quality of life
Commonly associated with allergic conjunctivitis, asthma and eczema as part of the atopic spectrum
Examination typically reveals pale, boggy, oedematous nasal mucosa with clear secretions, and children may show an allergic salute crease and allergic shiners
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by skin prick testing or specific IgE assays to identify triggers
Management principles begin with allergen avoidance and saline measures, then intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines according to severity
Poorly controlled disease contributes to sinusitis, otitis media with effusion, sleep disturbance and reduced school or work performance
Immunotherapy may be considered for confirmed single-allergen sensitivity that is inadequately controlled by standard therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammatory response of the nasal mucosa to inhaled allergens. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells, triggering an early-phase release of histamine and other mediators that produce sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea and congestion within minutes. A late-phase reaction, driven by recruited eosinophils, basophils and T cells, sustains mucosal inflammation and congestion hours later and heightens nasal reactivity. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema and hyperresponsiveness, and shared airway inflammation links the condition to asthma.
additionalDifferentials: Rhinitis medicamentosa from overuse of decongestant sprays
Structural causes such as deviated nasal septum
additionalInvestigations: Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to assess mucosa and exclude polyps
Skin prick testing to identify causative allergens
Serum allergen-specific IgE testing where skin testing is unsuitable
Nasal smear for eosinophils in selected cases
Assessment for coexisting asthma and sinus disease
redFlags: Unilateral nasal symptoms, bleeding or a mass suggesting a tumour or foreign body
Progressive obstruction with facial pain and purulent discharge indicating complicated sinusitis
Anosmia or orbital or visual symptoms requiring further evaluation
Symptoms of poorly controlled coexisting asthma
reference.prognosis: Allergic rhinitis is generally a chronic but benign condition; with allergen avoidance and appropriate pharmacotherapy most patients achieve good symptom control, though it may persist for years and contribute to comorbidities.
pitfalls: Missing coexisting asthma that needs concurrent treatment
Encouraging prolonged use of topical decongestants leading to rebound rhinitis
Attributing unilateral or bloodstained symptoms to allergy rather than investigating for tumour or foreign body
Underusing intranasal corticosteroids, the most effective agents, in moderate to severe disease
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Begin with allergen avoidance and nasal saline irrigation to reduce mucosal exposure and symptoms
Use intranasal corticosteroids as the mainstay for moderate-to-severe or persistent symptoms
Add oral or intranasal antihistamines for sneezing, itching and rhinorrhoea, using an intranasal antihistamine and corticosteroid combination when control is inadequate
Consider a leukotriene receptor antagonist, particularly where asthma coexists
Treat associated allergic conjunctivitis with ocular antihistamines or mast-cell stabilisers and coordinate asthma management
Refer for allergen immunotherapy, subcutaneous or sublingual, in confirmed refractory single-allergen disease
Refer to ENT or allergy services for diagnostic uncertainty, nasal polyps or treatment failure
